newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Politics affecting NZ property market - REINZ.
newsitem.headline: Politics affecting NZ property market - REINZ.

text.p: Indecision about the future direction of the government is clearly having an impact on the property market, the Real Estate Institute of New Zealand (REINZ) said on Friday.
Releasing its October sales figures, the REINZ said home buyers had yet to respond to recent cuts in mortgage rates.
A total of 6868 sales were reported by REINZ members in October -- an increase of 268 from the previous month, but down from the 7787 homes sold in October last year.
REINZ vice president Max Oliver said sales usually rose in the spring as more homes came on to the market.
"While lower (mortgage) rates have been announced by lending institutions, indecision about the future direction of government is clearly having an impact on sales," he said.
"In addition, buyers are becoming more selective and appear under no pressure to make a final decision to buy."

Oliver said the median price for a home nationwide of NZ$155,000 in October had returned to the same level as last March and compared with $142,000 in October 1995. The median sale price in September was $153,000.
In Auckland the median sale price was $223,000 in October compared with $220,000 in September and $195,000 in October 1995.
Sales in the Auckland region showed a slight increase from the previous month to reach 2352 from 2282 in September.
Oliver said realistically-priced properties were continuing to sell.
"However, most buyers are very cautious in their assessment of value and are not willing to pay inflated prices to unrealistic vendors," Oliver said.
He said median prices had increased in most districts from the previous month except in Manawatu and Southland, while Taranaki remained constant at a median price of $95,000.
Hawke's Bay, Taranaki and the Manawatu/Wanganui reported a degree of reluctance by buyers to commit themselves until the current political uncertainty had been resolved.
Wellington reported an improving market, which was expected to continue. Good homes in good localities were regularly attracting more than one offer.
In the South Island, only the Canterbury/Westland area reported hesitation in the market, although there were already signs of improvement.
